subject: Convergence for rare species in community occupancy

messages.author: 0549e8f4a843b6d4
messages.subject: Convergence for rare species in community occupancy
parts:
Hi,
I am working on a community occupancy model from a dataset of rodents trapped in grids of 50 traps clustered in 9 sites, and 3 habitats within sites (along a deforestation gradient) (27 grids of 50 traps total). I also repeated the same desig at 2 different seasons (wet/dry). I am trying to model change in species richness across the gradient, using a bayesian community occupancy model (and a meta-analysis of the richness, inspired by Chp 11 of AHM book). 
I have random intercepts for species, and sites, and random slopes across species for the effect of habitat and season (and their interactions). My issue is: of the 14 species captured, 3 represent 95% of captures, with some of the species only captured a handful of times, and mostly in 1 of the 3 habitat types... When I run the model, I get good convergence for the 3 predominant species, but not for the rare species. Given the end goal is to look at diversity, it would make no sense to remove rare species, so wondering if anyone would have advice or reference to point me to. At the end of the day, my derived parameters for the number of species per site all have Rhat<1.1, but fairly low effective size compared to more abundant species.... just wondering if this is something you just have to accept in this kind of model or if there is a way around it.

Thanks
Mathieu

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: Convergence for rare species in community occupancy
parts:
Dear Mathieu,

 

from a pragmatic point of view I’d be happy when all Rhat’s of the key params (= main structural params, plus derived params of interest, such as N in your case) are below that widely accepted threshold of 1.1. Of course, if you can push it even lower by running 2 days instead of 1, then that looks better. But in terms of the inferences at least about the posterior means, it typically makes hardly any difference in an MCMC run whether you have Rhat’s of, say, 1.5 or of 1.05 (but note that by this I don’t want to say that one should accept MCMC runs with Rhat’s that are larger than 1.1 …. And I also note that it may make more of a difference for variances and CRIs).

 

There are two things I am always unsure in such a community analysis:

  1. How good the estimates of N are when the information is so skewed as in your case. This paper may be of interest: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.4821. At any rate, I would strongly suggest not to “blindly” data-augment, but take as the maximum possible community size the “known” number of species that could possibly occur in your region, as taken from some field guide or local fauna.
  2. In a two-step analysis of species richness, we might want to put as much covariate information as possible into the first-step (community) model to get as unbiased estimates as possible. However, in the second step we then also want to put some of the key covariates, such as your deforestation gradient, into the model for the estimated N’s. I feel that something may be wrong here, because we are using some information twice…. But I don’t know how to proceed in an optimal way.

 

Please also note that there are variants of these community models that reparameterize the data augmentation part such that species richness becomes an actual parameter (however, this would then be tantamount to “blind data augmentation”). See these papers:

    • Royle, J.A., Converse, S.J., 2014. Hierarchical spatial capture-recapture models: modelling population density in stratified populations. Methods Ecol. Evol. 5, 37-43.
    • Royle, J.A., Converse, S.J., Link,W.A., 2012. Data augmentation for hierarchical capture-recapture models. arXiv preprint arXiv:1211.5706.
    • https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12536

 

Best regards  --- Marc
